q: Butyl iodide, CH₃CH₂CH₂CH₂I, has the IUPAC name:
x: The four-carbon chain is numbered from the end nearer the iodine, giving 1-iodobutane. Numbering from the other end (4-iodo) does not give the lowest locant.

q: The compound CH₂Cl₂, commonly called methylene chloride, is named in the IUPAC system as:
x: It is methane with two hydrogens replaced by chlorine, so it is dichloromethane. Methene does not exist as a parent name, and the compound has only one carbon, so it is not an ethane.

q: Using IUPAC rules, (CH₃)₂CHCH₂CH₂Br should be named:
x: The longest chain has four carbons. Numbering from the CH₂Br end gives locants 1 and 3, lower than 2 and 4 from the other end. The chain is butane, not pentane, because one CH₃ is a branch.

q: By IUPAC rules, CH₃CHBrCHBrCH₃ is named:
x: The chain has four carbons with bromine on the second and third carbons, giving 2,3-dibromobutane. Propane would have only three carbons.

q: Chloropropane, C₃H₇Cl, can exist as how many structural isomers?
x: Chlorine can be on an end carbon (1-chloropropane) or the middle carbon (2-chloropropane). Putting it on the other end carbon gives the same 1-chloropropane again.

q: In which compound is the chlorine atom bonded to a carbon that is attached to only one other carbon atom (a primary alkyl halide)?
x: In 1-chloro-2-methylpropane, (CH₃)₂CHCH₂Cl, the CH₂Cl carbon is bonded to one other carbon, so it is primary. 2-Chlorobutane and 2-chloropropane are secondary, and 2-chloro-2-methylpropane is tertiary.

q: Isopropyl chloride is the common name of the alkyl halide whose IUPAC name is:
x: The isopropyl group is (CH₃)₂CH–, so isopropyl chloride is (CH₃)₂CHCl, 2-chloropropane. 1-Chloropropane is n-propyl chloride.

q: Applying IUPAC rules, including alphabetical order when locants tie, CH₃CHBrCH(CH₃)CH₃ is named:
x: The longest chain has four carbons, and either direction gives the locants 2 and 3. When locants tie, the substituent first in alphabetical order (bromo) gets the lower number.

q: For the carbon–halogen bonds, the correct order of bond strength (bond enthalpy) is:
x: As the halogen atom gets larger, the C–X bond gets longer and weaker, so C–F is the strongest and C–I the weakest. The reversed order is the common slip.

q: Chloroethane, bromoethane and iodoethane have the same alkyl group. Their boiling points increase in the order:
x: Heavier, larger halogens give larger molecules with stronger London (van der Waals) forces, so the boiling point rises from the chloro to the iodo compound.

q: Which carbon–halogen bond is the shortest?
x: Fluorine has the smallest atomic radius of the halogens, so the C–F bond is the shortest. The bond length increases down the group to C–I.

q: Which statement about the physical properties of alkyl halides is correct?
o: They form strong hydrogen bonds with water
Their boiling points fall as the halogen becomes heavier
Bromoalkanes and iodoalkanes are generally denser than water
They boil lower than alkanes with the same number of carbons
x: Heavy bromine and iodine atoms make these compounds denser than water. Alkyl halides cannot hydrogen-bond with water, their boiling points rise with a heavier halogen, and they boil higher than the parent alkanes.

q: In which bond does the carbon atom carry the smallest partial positive charge?
x: Iodine is the least electronegative halogen, so the C–I bond is the least polar and its carbon is the least positive. Fluorine, the most electronegative, gives the largest partial charge.

q: Bromoethane is warmed with aqueous potassium hydroxide. The main organic product is:
x: In water, OH⁻ acts as a nucleophile and replaces the bromine, giving CH₃CH₂OH. Ethene is the main product with alcoholic KOH instead.

q: Bromoethane reacts with alcoholic potassium cyanide, KCN. The organic product and the change in the carbon chain are:
o: CH₃CH₂CN; chain longer by one carbon
CH₃CN; chain shorter by one carbon
x: CN⁻ replaces Br⁻, giving propanenitrile, CH₃CH₂CN. The carbon of the CN group adds one carbon to the chain, which is why this reaction is used to step up a chain.

q: In the SN1 mechanism, the slow, rate-determining step is:
o: Attack of the nucleophile on the carbocation
Simultaneous bond making and bond breaking
Ionisation of the C–X bond to give a carbocation and X⁻
Removal of a proton from the β-carbon
x: SN1 has two steps: the slow heterolysis of C–X to form a carbocation, then fast attack by the nucleophile. Simultaneous bond making and breaking describes SN2.

q: In the transition state of an SN2 reaction of CH₃Br with OH⁻, the central carbon atom is:
o: Fully bonded to OH, with Br already gone
A planar carbocation with no nucleophile attached
Part of a stable carbanion intermediate
Partly bonded to both the OH group and the Br atom
x: In SN2 the C–O bond forms while the C–Br bond breaks, so in the transition state the carbon is partly bonded to both. A carbocation belongs to SN1, and SN2 has no intermediate.

q: Tertiary alkyl halides such as (CH₃)₃CBr react extremely slowly by the SN2 mechanism because:
o: The C–Br bond in them is too strong to break
The bulky methyl groups block attack from the back of the carbon
They have no hydrogen on the β-carbon
x: SN2 needs the nucleophile to approach from the side opposite the halogen, and three alkyl groups crowd that side (steric hindrance). Tertiary carbocations are in fact the most stable.

q: Tertiary alkyl halides react readily by the SN1 mechanism mainly because:
o: The tertiary carbon is the least hindered for backside attack
The tertiary carbocation is stabilised by electron release from three alkyl groups
The nucleophile concentration controls their rate
Tertiary alkyl halides have the strongest C–X bond
x: SN1 depends on forming a carbocation, and the three alkyl groups push electrons towards the positive carbon (+I effect), making it stable. Backside attack belongs to SN2.

q: An alkyl halide is hydrolysed by the SN1 mechanism. If [RX] is tripled and [OH⁻] is doubled at the same time, the rate becomes:
x: For SN1, rate = k[RX], so only the alkyl halide concentration matters and the rate rises 3 times. Six times wrongly includes the [OH⁻] term.

q: In the name SN1, the number 1 shows that:
o: The reaction is completed in a single step
The nucleophile carries a charge of −1
Only one species, the alkyl halide, takes part in the rate-determining step
x: The 1 means unimolecular: the slow step involves only RX ionising. SN1 actually takes two steps, so a single step is wrong.

q: (CH₃)₃CBr is warmed with water and undergoes SN1 hydrolysis. The organic product is:
x: The tertiary carbocation (CH₃)₃C⁺ is attacked by water, giving (CH₃)₃COH, 2-methylpropan-2-ol. The OH ends up on the same carbon that carried the bromine; 2-methylpropene would be an elimination product.

q: In the reaction CH₃CH₂I + OH⁻ → CH₃CH₂OH + I⁻, the nucleophile and the leaving group are:
o: OH⁻ is the nucleophile and I⁻ is the leaving group
I⁻ is the nucleophile and OH⁻ is the leaving group
CH₃CH₂I is the nucleophile and OH⁻ is the leaving group
CH₃CH₂OH is the nucleophile and I⁻ is the leaving group
x: OH⁻ donates an electron pair to the carbon bonded to iodine, and iodine leaves as I⁻. The alkyl halide is the substrate, not the nucleophile.

q: In dehydrohalogenation of an alkyl halide, the hydrogen atom removed along with the halogen comes from:
o: The α-carbon, which bears the halogen
The β-carbon, next to the carbon bearing the halogen
Any carbon at the far end of the chain
The base used in the reaction
x: The H and X are lost from neighbouring carbons (β-elimination), so a C=C double bond forms between the α- and β-carbons.

q: 2-Bromobutane is heated with alcoholic KOH. According to Saytzeff's rule, the main product is:
x: Saytzeff's rule says the more substituted alkene is the main product, so H is lost from C-3 to give CH₃CH=CHCH₃. But-1-ene forms too but in smaller amount; butan-2-ol would need aqueous KOH.

q: An alkyl halide undergoes elimination by the E1 mechanism. If the base concentration is doubled while [RX] stays the same, the rate:
x: In E1 the slow step is ionisation of RX alone, so rate = k[RX] and the base does not appear in the rate equation. Doubling would be true for E2.

q: When alcoholic KOH converts an alkyl halide into an alkene, the hydroxide or ethoxide ion acts as a:
o: Nucleophile, attacking the carbon bonded to the halogen
x: In elimination the ion pulls off a β-hydrogen as H⁺, so it acts as a base. Attacking the carbon bonded to the halogen is its role in substitution.

q: Elimination of one molecule of HCl from C₄H₉Cl gives an organic product with the molecular formula:
x: Removing H and Cl from C₄H₉Cl leaves C₄H₈, a butene. C₄H₉OH would be the substitution product.

q: Ignoring cis–trans isomers, which alkyl halide gives only one alkene when heated with alcoholic KOH?
x: In 3-bromopentane both β-carbons are equivalent, so only pent-2-ene forms. Each of the others has two different β-carbons and gives two alkenes, for example but-1-ene and but-2-ene from 2-bromobutane.

q: Bromoethane heated with concentrated alcoholic KOH loses HBr mainly by which mechanism?
x: Bromoethane is primary, and a primary carbocation is too unstable for E1, so the strong base removes H while Br leaves in one step (E2). SN1 and SN2 are substitutions, not loss of HBr.
